S6.3 Example

Here we provide an example to illustrate the difference among the SDP bound ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} (Eq.(S27)), the analytical bound ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A}, and the bound obtained from the Ozawa’s relation, ℰO​z​a​w​a\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa}.

Take ρ\rho and three observables, X1X_{1}, X2X_{2}, X3X_{3} as

ρ=(p20001−p000p2),X1=(010101010),\displaystyle\rho=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{p}{2}&0&0\\ 0&1-p&0\\ 0&0&\frac{p}{2}\end{pmatrix},\ X_{1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&0&1\\ 0&1&0\end{pmatrix}, (S86)
X2=(0−i0i0−i0i0),X3=(10000000−1).\displaystyle X_{2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i&0\\ i&0&-i\\ 0&i&0\end{pmatrix},\ X_{3}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\ 0&0&0\\ 0&0&-1\end{pmatrix}.

Here X1X_{1}, X2X_{2}, X3X_{3} are the spin-1 operators with [Xj,Xk]≠0[X_{j},X_{k}]\neq 0 for all j≠kj\neq k. In this case we have (Δ​X1)2=(Δ​X2)2=2−p(\Delta X_{1})^{2}=(\Delta X_{2})^{2}=2-p, (Δ​X3)2=p(\Delta X_{3})^{2}=p, and

c12\displaystyle c_{12} =12​‖ρ​[X1,X2]​ρ‖1=p,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\|\sqrt{\rho}[X_{1},X_{2}]\sqrt{\rho}\|_{1}=p, (S87)
c23\displaystyle c_{23} =12​‖ρ​[X2,X3]​ρ‖1=p⁡(1−p),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\|\sqrt{\rho}[X_{2},X_{3}]\sqrt{\rho}\|_{1}=\sqrt{p(1-p)},
c31\displaystyle c_{31} =12​‖ρ​[X3,X1]​ρ‖1=p⁡(1−p).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\|\sqrt{\rho}[X_{3},X_{1}]\sqrt{\rho}\|_{1}=\sqrt{p(1-p)}.

For the simultaneous measurement of (X1,X2)(X_{1},X_{2}), (X2,X3)(X_{2},X_{3}), (X3,X1)(X_{3},X_{1}), the Ozawa’s relation gives

ϵ12+ϵ22\displaystyle\epsilon_{1}^{2}+\epsilon_{2}^{2} ≥ℰO​z​a​w​a​(X1,X2)=2−p−2​1−p,\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa}(X_{1},X_{2})=2-p-2\sqrt{1-p}, (S88)
ϵ22+ϵ32\displaystyle\epsilon_{2}^{2}+\epsilon_{3}^{2} ≥ℰO​z​a​w​a​(X2,X3)=1−1−p⁡(1−p),\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa}(X_{2},X_{3})=1-\sqrt{1-p(1-p)},
ϵ32+ϵ12\displaystyle\epsilon_{3}^{2}+\epsilon_{1}^{2} ≥ℰO​z​a​w​a​(X3,X1)=1−1−p⁡(1−p).\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa}(X_{3},X_{1})=1-\sqrt{1-p(1-p)}.

While ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} can be calculated by substituting {|uq⟩}\{|u_{q}\rangle\} with the eigenvectors of ρ​[Xj,Xk]​ρ\sqrt{\rho}[X_{j},X_{k}]\sqrt{\rho}. Specifically for (X2,X3)(X_{2},X_{3}), we have |u0⟩=(1,2,1)T/2|u_{0}\rangle=(1,\sqrt{2},1)^{T}/2, |u1⟩=(1,−2,1)T/2|u_{1}\rangle=(1,-\sqrt{2},1)^{T}/2, |u2⟩=(1,0,−1)T/2|u_{2}\rangle=(1,0,-1)^{T}/\sqrt{2}, which gives

ϵ22+ϵ32≥ℰA​(X2,X3)=∑q=0212​λq​(αq−αq2−βq2)\displaystyle\epsilon_{2}^{2}+\epsilon_{3}^{2}\geq\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{2},X_{3})=\sum_{q=0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{q}\left(\alpha_{q}-\sqrt{\alpha_{q}^{2}-\beta_{q}^{2}}\right) (S89)
=2−p4​(4−3​p2−p−(4−3​p2−p)2−(4​p⁡(1−p)2−p)2)\displaystyle=\frac{2-p}{4}\left(\frac{4-3p}{2-p}-\sqrt{\left(\frac{4-3p}{2-p}\right)^{2}-\left(\frac{4\sqrt{p(1-p)}}{2-p}\right)^{2}}\right)
=14​(4−3​p−|4−5​p|).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4}(4-3p-|4-5p|).

Similarly for (X1,X2)(X_{1},X_{2}) and (X3,X1)(X_{3},X_{1}), we have

ϵ12+ϵ22\displaystyle\epsilon_{1}^{2}+\epsilon_{2}^{2} ≥ℰA​(X1,X2)=p,\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{1},X_{2})=p, (S90)
ϵ32+ϵ12\displaystyle\epsilon_{3}^{2}+\epsilon_{1}^{2} ≥ℰA​(X3,X1)=14​(4−3​p−|4−5​p|).\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{3},X_{1})=\frac{1}{4}(4-3p-|4-5p|).

In Fig. S6, we illustrate the comparisons among the three bounds: (i) ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} that can be computed with SDP; (ii) ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} that can be analytically obtained and (iii) ℰO​z​a​w​a\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa} that obtained from the Ozawa’s relation. It can be seen that for the simultaneous measurement of two observables, we already have ℰ0>ℰA>ℰO​z​a​w​a\mathcal{E}_{0}>\mathcal{E}_{A}>\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa}. While for the simultaneous measurement of three observables, the SDP bound is tighter than the bound obtained by simply adding the results for each pairs of the observables.

S7 Comparison of the analytical bound for more than two observables with the Ozawa’s bound on pure states

We have shown that in the case of two observables, ℰA=ℰO​z​a​w​a\mathcal{E}_{A}=\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa} for pure states and ℰA≥ℰO​z​a​w​a\mathcal{E}_{A}\geq\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa} for mixed states. Thus for mixed states we already get tighter analytical bound than the Ozawa’s bound. In this section we show that for pure states the analytical bound obtained for an arbitrary number of observables,

Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)≥(‖SRe−12​S~Im​SRe−12‖F+1−1)2,\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}})\geq\left(\sqrt{\|S_{\text{Re}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}S_{\text{Re}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_{F}+1}-1\right)^{2}, (S91)

is always tighter than the simple summation of the Ozawa’s bound when the number of observables is bigger than 4 (n≥5n\geq 5).

Since Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}}) does not change under linear transformations, without loss of generality, we can assume SRe=IS_{\text{Re}}=I, the bound then becomes

∑jϵj2≥(‖S~Im‖F+1−1)2.\sum_{j}\epsilon_{j}^{2}\geq\left(\sqrt{\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1}-1\right)^{2}. (S92)

For pure state ρ=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|, with arbitrary {|uq⟩}\{|u_{q}\rangle\} we have (Suq)j​k=⟨ψ|Xj​Xk|ψ⟩​|⟨ψ|uq⟩|2(S_{u_{q}})_{jk}=\langle\psi|X_{j}X_{k}|\psi\rangle|\langle\psi|u_{q}\rangle|^{2}, and (Suq,Im)j​k=12​i​⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩​|⟨ψ|uq⟩|2(S_{u_{q},\text{Im}})_{jk}=\frac{1}{2i}\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|\langle\psi|u_{q}\rangle|^{2}. The matrices Suq,ImS_{u_{q},\text{Im}} for different qq then equal to a common antisymmetric matrix multiplied by non-negative numbers |⟨ψ|uq⟩|2|\langle\psi|u_{q}\rangle|^{2}. In this case the optimal choice is not to take any transpose. With arbitrary {|uq⟩}\{|u_{q}\rangle\} with ∑q|uq⟩​⟨uq|=I\sum_{q}|u_{q}\rangle\langle u_{q}|=I, we have ∑q|⟨ψ|uq⟩|2=1\sum_{q}|\langle\psi|u_{q}\rangle|^{2}=1, and

(S~Im)j​k=∑q(Suq,Im)j​k=∑q12​i​⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|⟨ψ⁡|uq⟩|2=12​i​⟨ψ​|[Xj,Xk]|​ψ⟩(\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}})_{jk}=\sum_{q}(S_{u_{q},\text{Im}})_{jk}=\sum_{q}\frac{1}{2i}\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|\langle\psi|u_{q}\rangle|^{2}=\frac{1}{2i}\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle (S93)

From the Ozawa’s relation, we show in Appendix S6.2 that

w1​ϵj2+w2​ϵk2≥ℰO​z​a​w​a≡12​(α−α2−β2),w_{1}\epsilon_{j}^{2}+w_{2}\epsilon_{k}^{2}\geq\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa}\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha-\sqrt{\alpha^{2}-\beta^{2}}\right), (S94)

where α=w1​(Δ​Xj)2+w2​(Δ​Xk)2\alpha=w_{1}(\Delta X_{j})^{2}+w_{2}(\Delta X_{k})^{2}, β=w1​w2​‖ρ​[Xj,Xk]​ρ‖1\beta=\sqrt{w_{1}w_{2}}\|\sqrt{\rho}[X_{j},X_{k}]\sqrt{\rho}\|_{1}. For the comparison we choose w1=w2=1w_{1}=w_{2}=1 and for normalized observables with SRe=IS_{\text{Re}}=I we have (Δ​Xj)2=1(\Delta X_{j})^{2}=1, ∀j\forall j. For pure state, ρ=|ψ⟩​⟨ψ|\rho=|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|, the Ozawa’s bound is then given by

ϵj2+ϵk2≥ℰO​z​a​w​a​(Xj,Xk)≡12​(2−4−|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2)=1−1−12​|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2,\epsilon_{j}^{2}+\epsilon_{k}^{2}\geq\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa}(X_{j},X_{k})\equiv\frac{1}{2}\left(2-\sqrt{4-|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2}}\right)=1-\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{2}|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2}}, (S95)

By summing all pairs, we obtain

∑lϵl2≥1n−1​∑j,k(1−1−12​|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2).\sum_{l}\epsilon_{l}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j,k}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{2}|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2}}\right). (S96)

Since 1−12​|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2≤11-\frac{1}{2}|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2}\leq 1, we have 1−12​|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2≥1−12​|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{2}|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2}}\geq 1-\frac{1}{2}|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2} and

∑j,k(1−1−12​|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2)≤∑j,k12​|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2=12​‖S~Im‖F2.\sum_{j,k}\left(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{2}|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2}}\right)\leq\sum_{j,k}\frac{1}{2}|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}^{2}. (S97)

The bound in Eq.(S92) is then tighter than the bound in Eq.(S96) when

(‖S~Im‖F+1−1)2≥12​(n−1)​‖S~Im‖F2≥1n−1​∑j,k(1−1−12​|⟨ψ|[Xj,Xk]|ψ⟩|2).\left(\sqrt{\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1}-1\right)^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2(n-1)}\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j,k}(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{1}{2}|\langle\psi|[X_{j},X_{k}]|\psi\rangle|^{2}}). (S98)

The first inequality is equivalent to

‖S~Im‖F+1−1≥12​(n−1)​‖S~Im‖F⇔12​(n−1)​(‖S~Im‖F+1)−12​(n−1)−‖S~Im‖F+1+1≤0⇔(‖S~Im‖F+1)−2​(n−1)​‖S~Im‖F+1+2​(n−1)−1≤0⇔(‖S~Im‖F+1−n−12)2−n−12+2​(n−1)−1≤0⇔(‖S~Im‖F+1−n−12)2≤(n−12−1)2⇔n−12−(n−12−1)≤‖S~Im‖F+1≤n−12+(n−12−1)⇔1≤‖S~Im‖F+1≤(2​(n−1)−1)2⇔0≤‖S~Im‖F≤2​(n−1)−2​2​(n−1),\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\sqrt{\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1}-1\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2(n-1)}}\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}\\ \Leftrightarrow\quad&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2(n-1)}}(\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1)-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2(n-1)}}-\sqrt{\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1}+1\leq 0\\ \Leftrightarrow\quad&(\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1)-\sqrt{2(n-1)}\sqrt{\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1}+\sqrt{2(n-1)}-1\leq 0\\ \Leftrightarrow\quad&\left(\sqrt{\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1}-\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{2}}\right)^{2}-\frac{n-1}{2}+\sqrt{2(n-1)}-1\leq 0\\ \Leftrightarrow\quad&\left(\sqrt{\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1}-\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{2}}\right)^{2}\leq\left(\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{2}}-1\right)^{2}\\ \Leftrightarrow\quad&\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{2}}-\left(\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{2}}-1\right)\leq\sqrt{\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1}\leq\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{2}}+\left(\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{2}}-1\right)\\ \Leftrightarrow\quad&1\leq\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}+1\leq(\sqrt{2(n-1)}-1)^{2}\\ \Leftrightarrow\quad&0\leq\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}\leq 2(n-1)-2\sqrt{2(n-1)},\end{aligned} (S99)

this always holds when n≥5n\geq 5 since from SRe=IS_{\text{Re}}=I and SRe+i​S~Im≥0S_{\text{Re}}+i\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\geq 0 we have ‖S~Im‖F≤‖SRe‖F=n\|\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}\|_{F}\leq\|S_{\text{Re}}\|_{F}=\sqrt{n}, and n≤2​(n−1)−2​2​(n−1)\sqrt{n}\leq 2(n-1)-2\sqrt{2(n-1)} when n≥5n\geq 5. Thus for n≥5n\geq 5 observables on pure states, the bound in Eq.(S92) is always tighter than the simple summation of Ozawa’s relation for all pairs of the observables. We note that for pure states, ℰA=ℰO​z​a​w​a\mathcal{E}_{A}=\mathcal{E}_{Ozawa}, the bound in Eq.(S92) is thus also tighter than the simple summation of ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} for all pairs.

S8 Comparison of the SDP bound for more than two observables with the Ozawa’s bound on mixed states

For general nn observables, {X1,⋯,Xn}\{X_{1},\cdots,X_{n}\}, we can use the results on two observables to show that the SDP bound for ∑i=1nϵi2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}^{2} is always tighter than the bound obtained by simply summing up the Ozawa’s relation for all ϵj2+ϵk2\epsilon_{j}^{2}+\epsilon_{k}^{2}.

First note that for any pair of observables, we have ℰ0​(Xj,Xk)≥∑qλq​ℰ|ϕq⟩​(Xj,Xk)\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{j},X_{k})\geq\sum_{q}\lambda_{q}\mathcal{E}_{|\phi_{q}\rangle}(X_{j},X_{k}), and ∑qλq​ℰ|ϕq⟩​(Xj,Xk)\sum_{q}\lambda_{q}\mathcal{E}_{|\phi_{q}\rangle}(X_{j},X_{k}) is tighter than the bound obtained from the Ozawa’s relation. Thus the SDP bound for two observables is already tighter than the bound obtained from the Ozawa’s relation. As ∑i=1nϵi2=1n−1​∑j≠k(ϵj2+ϵk2)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}^{2}=\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq k}(\epsilon_{j}^{2}+\epsilon_{k}^{2}), we can use the bound on two observables to obtain a bound on ∑i=1nϵi2\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}^{2} as ∑i=1nϵi2≥1n−1​∑j≠kℰ0​(Xj,Xk)\sum_{i=1}^{n}\epsilon_{i}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq k}\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{j},X_{k}). This is tighter than the bound by summing up the Ozawa’s relation for all pairs since each ℰ0​(Xj,Xk)\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{j},X_{k}) is tighter. To show the SDP bound for nn observables is tighter than the bound obtained by summing up the Ozawa’s relation, we just need to show

ℰ0​(X1,⋯,Xn)≥1n−1​∑j≠kℰ0​(Xj,Xk).\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{1},\cdots,X_{n})\geq\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq k}\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{j},X_{k}). (S100)

By taking W=InW=I_{n} with InI_{n} as n×nn\times n Identity matrix, we have

ℰ0​(X1,⋯,Xn)=min𝕊,{Rj}j=1nTr[(I⊗ρ)(𝕊−ℝ𝕏†−𝕏ℝ†+𝕏𝕏†)|𝕊≥ℝℝ†,𝕊j​k=𝕊k​j=𝕊j​k†,Rj=Rj†]=Tr⁡[(I⊗ρ)​(𝕊∗−ℝ∗​𝕏†−𝕏ℝ∗⁣†+𝕏𝕏†)]=1n−1​∑j,kTr⁡[(I(j,k)⊗ρ)​(𝕊∗−ℝ∗​𝕏†−𝕏ℝ∗⁣†+𝕏𝕏†)],\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{1},\cdots,X_{n})\\ =&\min_{\mathbb{S},\{R_{j}\}_{j=1}^{n}}\mathrm{Tr}[(I\otimes\rho)(\mathbb{S}-\mathbb{R}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger}-\mathbb{X}\mathbb{R}^{\dagger}+\mathbb{X}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger})\\ &\quad|\mathbb{S}\geq\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^{\dagger},\mathbb{S}_{jk}=\mathbb{S}_{kj}=\mathbb{S}_{jk}^{\dagger},R_{j}=R_{j}^{\dagger}]\\ =&\mathrm{Tr}[(I\otimes\rho)(\mathbb{S}^{*}-\mathbb{R}^{*}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger}-\mathbb{X}\mathbb{R}^{*\dagger}+\mathbb{X}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger})]\\ =&\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j,k}\mathrm{Tr}[(I^{(j,k)}\otimes\rho)(\mathbb{S}^{*}-\mathbb{R}^{*}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger}-\mathbb{X}\mathbb{R}^{*\dagger}+\mathbb{X}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger})],\end{aligned} (S101)

here 𝕊∗\mathbb{S}^{*} and ℝ∗\mathbb{R}^{*} denote the optimal operators that achieve the minimum for nn observables, I(j,k)I^{(j,k)} denote the diagonal matrix with its jjth and kkth diagonal element equal to 1 while others equal to 0. When W=I(j,k)W=I^{(j,k)}, only 2×22\times 2 blocks with indexes (j,k)(j,k) contribute and we have

Tr[(I(j,k)⊗ρ)(𝕊∗−ℝ∗𝕏†−𝕏ℝ∗⁣†+𝕏𝕏†)]=Tr[(I2⊗ρ)​(𝕊∗(j,k)−ℝ∗(j,k)​𝕏†(j,k)CLOSE−𝕏(j,k)ℝ∗(j,k)†+𝕏(j,k)𝕏†(j,k))]\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \mathrm{Tr}[&(I^{(j,k)}\otimes\rho)(\mathbb{S}^{*}-\mathbb{R}^{*}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger}-\mathbb{X}\mathbb{R}^{*\dagger}+\mathbb{X}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger})]\\ =\mathrm{Tr}[&(I_{2}\otimes\rho)(\mathbb{S}^{*(j,k)}-\mathbb{R}^{*(j,k)}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger(j,k)}\\ &-\mathbb{X}^{(j,k)}\mathbb{R}^{*(j,k)\dagger}+\mathbb{X}^{(j,k)}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger(j,k)})]\end{aligned} (S102)

here I2I_{2} is 2×22\times 2 Identity matrix, 𝕊∗(j,k)=(𝕊j​j∗𝕊j​k∗𝕊k​j∗𝕊k​k∗)\mathbb{S}^{*(j,k)}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{S}_{jj}^{*}&\mathbb{S}_{jk}^{*}\\ \mathbb{S}_{kj}^{*}&\mathbb{S}_{kk}^{*}\end{pmatrix}, ℝ∗(j,k)=(Rj∗Rk∗)†\mathbb{R}^{*(j,k)}=\begin{pmatrix}R_{j}^{*}&R_{k}^{*}\end{pmatrix}^{\dagger}, 𝕏(j,k)=(XjXk)†\mathbb{X}^{(j,k)}=\begin{pmatrix}X_{j}&X_{k}\end{pmatrix}^{\dagger}. Note that 𝕊j​k∗=𝕊k​j∗=𝕊j​k∗⁣†\mathbb{S}_{jk}^{*}=\mathbb{S}_{kj}^{*}=\mathbb{S}_{jk}^{*\dagger} for each (j,k)(j,k), Rj∗=Rj∗⁣†R_{j}^{*}=R_{j}^{*\dagger} for each jj, and from 𝕊∗≥ℝ∗​ℝ∗⁣†\mathbb{S}^{*}\geq\mathbb{R}^{*}\mathbb{R}^{*\dagger}, we have

(𝕊j​j∗𝕊j​k∗𝕊k​j∗𝕊k​k∗)≥(Rj∗​Rj∗Rj∗​Rk∗Rk∗​Rj∗Rk∗​Rk∗),for each​(j,k).\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{S}_{jj}^{*}&\mathbb{S}_{jk}^{*}\\ \mathbb{S}_{kj}^{*}&\mathbb{S}_{kk}^{*}\end{pmatrix}\geq\begin{pmatrix}R_{j}^{*}R_{j}^{*}&R_{j}^{*}R_{k}^{*}\\ R_{k}^{*}R_{j}^{*}&R_{k}^{*}R_{k}^{*}\end{pmatrix},\ \text{for each}\ (j,k). (S103)

Thus Tr[(I2⊗ρ)(𝕊∗(j,k)−ℝ∗(j,k)𝕏†(j,k)−𝕏(j,k)ℝ∗(j,k)†+𝕏(j,k)𝕏†(j,k))]≥ℰ0(Xj,Xk)\mathrm{Tr}[(I_{2}\otimes\rho)(\mathbb{S}^{*(j,k)}-\mathbb{R}^{*(j,k)}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger(j,k)}-\mathbb{X}^{(j,k)}\mathbb{R}^{*(j,k)\dagger}+\mathbb{X}^{(j,k)}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger(j,k)})]\geq\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{j},X_{k}) since ℰ0(Xj,Xk)=min𝕊,ℝTr[(I2⊗ρ)(𝕊−ℝ𝕏†−𝕏ℝ†+𝕏𝕏†)\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{j},X_{k})=\min_{\mathbb{S},\mathbb{R}}\mathrm{Tr}[(I_{2}\otimes\rho)(\mathbb{S}-\mathbb{R}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger}-\mathbb{X}\mathbb{R}^{\dagger}+\mathbb{X}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger}), where 𝕏=(XjXk)†\mathbb{X}=\begin{pmatrix}X_{j}&X_{k}\end{pmatrix}^{\dagger} and the minimum is taken over all 𝕊=(𝕊j​j𝕊j​k𝕊k​j𝕊k​k)\mathbb{S}=\begin{pmatrix}\mathbb{S}_{jj}&\mathbb{S}_{jk}\\ \mathbb{S}_{kj}&\mathbb{S}_{kk}\end{pmatrix} and ℝ=(RjRk)†\mathbb{R}=\begin{pmatrix}R_{j}&R_{k}\end{pmatrix}^{\dagger} with 𝕊≥ℝℝ†,𝕊j​k=𝕊k​j=𝕊j​k†,Rj=Rj†\mathbb{S}\geq\mathbb{R}\mathbb{R}^{\dagger},\mathbb{S}_{jk}=\mathbb{S}_{kj}=\mathbb{S}_{jk}^{\dagger},R_{j}=R_{j}^{\dagger}. Thus

ℰ0​(X1,⋯,Xn)=1n−1​∑j≠kTr⁡[(I(j,k)⊗ρ)​(𝕊∗−ℝ∗​𝕏†−𝕏ℝ∗⁣†+𝕏𝕏†)]≥1n−1​∑j≠kℰ0​(Xj,Xk).\displaystyle\begin{aligned} &\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{1},\cdots,X_{n})\\ =&\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq k}\mathrm{Tr}[(I^{(j,k)}\otimes\rho)(\mathbb{S}^{*}-\mathbb{R}^{*}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger}-\mathbb{X}\mathbb{R}^{*\dagger}+\mathbb{X}\mathbb{X}^{\dagger})]\\ \geq&\frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{j\neq k}\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{j},X_{k}).\end{aligned} (S104)

Since ℰ0​(Xj,Xk)\mathcal{E}_{0}(X_{j},X_{k}) is tighter than the Ozawa’s relation, the SDP bound is thus always tighter than the bound obtained from the simple summation of the Ozawa’s relation for all pairs.

S9 Examples

In this section, we demonstrate the applications of (i) the bounds of Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}}); (ii) ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} that can be analytically obtained and (iii) ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} that can be computed with SDP in specific examples.

S9.1 Example: Error tradeoff relation for three observables on a qubit

Bounds obtained from Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}}):

Consider the approximate measurement of the three Pauli operators 12​σx\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{x}, 12​σy\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{y}, 12​σz\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{z} for a general spin-1/2 state ρ=12​(I+rx​σx+ry​σy+rz​σz)\rho=\frac{1}{2}(I+r_{x}\sigma_{x}+r_{y}\sigma_{y}+r_{z}\sigma_{z}), where |rx|2+|ry|2+|rz|2≤1|r_{x}|^{2}+|r_{y}|^{2}+|r_{z}|^{2}\leq 1. In this case X1=12​σxX_{1}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{x}, X2=12​σyX_{2}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{y}, X3=12​σzX_{3}=\frac{1}{2}\sigma_{z}, we have (SRe)j​k=12​Tr​(ρ⁡{Xj,Xk})=12​Tr​(ρ⋅12​δj​k​I)=14​δj​k(S_{\text{Re}})_{jk}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\rho\{X_{j},X_{k}\})=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Tr}(\rho\cdot\frac{1}{2}\delta_{jk}I)=\frac{1}{4}\delta_{jk} for 1≤j,k≤31\leq j,k\leq 3. Thus SRe=14​IS_{\text{Re}}=\frac{1}{4}I, the error tradeoff relation is then given by

ϵ12+ϵ22≥ℰA​(X1,X2)=14​(1−λ2).\epsilon_{1}^{2}+\epsilon_{2}^{2}\geq\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{1},X_{2})=\frac{1}{4}(1-\lambda^{2}). (S126)

Similarly for the simultaneous measurement of (X2,X3)(X_{2},X_{3}) and (X3,X1)(X_{3},X_{1}), the bound ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} can be calculated as

ϵ22+ϵ32\displaystyle\epsilon_{2}^{2}+\epsilon_{3}^{2} ≥ℰA​(X2,X3)=14,\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{2},X_{3})=\frac{1}{4}, (S127)
ϵ32+ϵ12\displaystyle\epsilon_{3}^{2}+\epsilon_{1}^{2} ≥ℰA​(X3,X1)=14​(1−λ2).\displaystyle\geq\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{3},X_{1})=\frac{1}{4}(1-\lambda^{2}).

For the simultaneous measurement of (X1,X2,X3)(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}), a direct summation of the bounds for each pairs of the observables gives

ϵ12+ϵ22+ϵ32≥12​(ℰA​(X1,X2)+ℰA​(X2,X3)+ℰA​(X3,X1))=18+14​(1−λ2).\epsilon_{1}^{2}+\epsilon_{2}^{2}+\epsilon_{3}^{2}\geq\frac{1}{2}(\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{1},X_{2})+\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{2},X_{3})+\mathcal{E}_{A}(X_{3},X_{1}))=\frac{1}{8}+\frac{1}{4}(1-\lambda^{2}). (S128)

The SDP ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} also gives a bound for (X1,X2,X3)(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3}) directly, which can be computed efficiently. In Fig. S7, we make comparisons among the three bounds, (i) bound that obtained from Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}}); (ii) the simple summation of the analytical bound ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} for all pairs and (iii) ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} that can be computed with SDP. It can be seen that the SDP bound is the tightest among the three bounds. We note that although the simple summation of ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} for each pairs of the observables is tighter than Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}}) in this example, there are cases the bound obtained from Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}}) can be tighter, as we have shown in the previous section.

S9.2 Example: Tradeoff relation for the estimation of multiple parameters in a qubit

Bounds obtained from Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}}):

The error-tradeoff relation for multiple observables can be used to obtain tradeoff relation in multiparameter quantum estimation. Here we consider the simultaneous estimation of the three parameters (λ,θ,φ)(\lambda,\theta,\varphi) in ρ=12​(I+rx​σx+ry​σy+rz​σz)\rho=\frac{1}{2}(I+r_{x}\sigma_{x}+r_{y}\sigma_{y}+r_{z}\sigma_{z}), where rx=λ​sin⁡θ​cos⁡φr_{x}=\lambda\sin\theta\cos\varphi, ry=λ​sin⁡θ​sin⁡φr_{y}=\lambda\sin\theta\sin\varphi, and rz=λ​cos⁡θr_{z}=\lambda\cos\theta, here |λ|≤1|\lambda|\leq 1.

For any measurement on ρ\rho, the classical Fisher information matrix, FCF_{C}, is bounded as

Tr⁡[FQ−1​FC]≤3−(‖FQ−12​S~Im​FQ−12‖F+1−1)2,\mathrm{Tr}[F_{Q}^{-1}F_{C}]\leq 3-\left(\sqrt{\|F_{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}F_{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\|_{F}+1}-1\right)^{2}, (S129)

The SLDs for (λ,θ,φ)(\lambda,\theta,\varphi) are given by

here n→=(sin⁡θ​cos⁡φ,sin⁡θ​sin⁡φ,cos⁡θ)\vec{n}=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta), σ→=(σx,σy,σz)\vec{\sigma}=(\sigma_{x},\sigma_{y},\sigma_{z}), and the quantum Fisher information matrix is

FQ=(11−λ2000λ2000λ2​sin2⁡θ).F_{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{1-\lambda^{2}}&0&0\\ 0&\lambda^{2}&0\\ 0&0&\lambda^{2}\sin^{2}\theta\end{pmatrix}. (S131)

We can use Eq.(S109) to maximize S~Im\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}} over {|uq⟩}\{|u_{q}\rangle\}. Note that under the reparameterization which makes FQ=IF_{Q}=I, we have FQ−12​S~Im​FQ−12=S~ImF_{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}F_{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}=\tilde{S}_{\text{Im}}. L~λ=11−λ2​(n→⋅σ→−λ​I),L~θ=∂θn→⋅σ→,L~φ=1|sin⁡θ|​(∂φn→⋅σ→).\tilde{L}_{\lambda}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\lambda^{2}}}(\vec{n}\cdot\vec{\sigma}-\lambda I),\quad\tilde{L}_{\theta}=\partial_{\theta}\vec{n}\cdot\vec{\sigma},\quad\tilde{L}_{\varphi}=\frac{1}{|\sin\theta|}(\partial_{\varphi}\vec{n}\cdot\vec{\sigma}). S9.3 Example: Tradeoff relation under collective measurement

While the tradeoff relation is obtained under local measurements, it can also be used to obtain tradeoff relations for collective measurements on pp copies of the states by simply replacing ρ\rho with ρx⊗p\rho_{x}^{\otimes p}.

As an example we consider the simultaneous estimation of the three parameters (λ,θ,φ)(\lambda,\theta,\varphi) in a state ρ=12​(I+rx​σx+ry​σy+rz​σz)\rho=\frac{1}{2}(I+r_{x}\sigma_{x}+r_{y}\sigma_{y}+r_{z}\sigma_{z}), where rx=λ​sin⁡θ​cos⁡φr_{x}=\lambda\sin\theta\cos\varphi, ry=λ​sin⁡θ​sin⁡φr_{y}=\lambda\sin\theta\sin\varphi, and rz=λ​cos⁡θr_{z}=\lambda\cos\theta, |λ|≤1|\lambda|\leq 1. But different from previous section, here we also allow collective measurement on two-copies of the state, ρ⊗ρ\rho\otimes\rho.

To obtain the tradeoff relation under the collective measurement on 2-copies of the state, we can simply treat ρ⊗ρ\rho\otimes\rho as a larger single state. Its SLDs are given by Lj​2=Lj⊗I+I⊗LjL_{j2}=L_{j}\otimes I+I\otimes L_{j} with j=λ,θ,φj=\lambda,\theta,\varphi and the quantum Fisher information matrix is FQ​2=2​FQF_{Q2}=2F_{Q} with FQF_{Q} as the quantum Fisher information matrix of a single ρ\rho.

If we choose {|uq⟩}\{|u_{q}\rangle\} as the computational basis with |u0⟩=|00⟩|u_{0}\rangle=|00\rangle, |u1⟩=|01⟩|u_{1}\rangle=|01\rangle, |u2⟩=|10⟩|u_{2}\rangle=|10\rangle, |u3⟩=|11⟩|u_{3}\rangle=|11\rangle, the corresponding Suq,Im​2S_{u_{q},\text{Im}2} are given by

Su1,Im​2\displaystyle S_{u_{1},\text{Im}2} =Su2,Im​2=(00λ2​cos⁡θ​sin2⁡θ2​1−λ200−12​λ3​sin3⁡θ−λ2​cos⁡θ​sin2⁡θ2​1−λ212​λ3​sin3⁡θ0)\displaystyle=S_{u_{2},\text{Im}2}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0&\frac{\lambda^{2}\cos\theta\sin^{2}\theta}{2\sqrt{1-\lambda^{2}}}\\ 0&0&-\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{3}\sin^{3}\theta\\ -\frac{\lambda^{2}\cos\theta\sin^{2}\theta}{2\sqrt{1-\lambda^{2}}}&\frac{1}{2}\lambda^{3}\sin^{3}\theta&0\end{pmatrix}

S9.4 Example: Tradeoff relation for the estimation of multiple parameters in three qubits

We provide an example with three qubits to show that the analytical bound obtained from Tr⁡(SRe−1​QRe)\mathrm{Tr}(S_{\text{Re}}^{-1}Q_{\text{Re}}) can be tighter than the simple summation over the bounds ℰA\mathcal{E}_{A} for each pairs of observables.

We consider a parameterized pure state |ψ⟩=sin⁡θ0​|ψ1⟩+cos⁡θ0​ei​ϕ0​|ψ2⟩|\psi\rangle=\sin\theta_{0}|\psi_{1}\rangle+\cos\theta_{0}e^{i\phi_{0}}|\psi_{2}\rangle, where

|ψ1⟩=sinθ1sinθ2|001⟩+sinθ1cosθ2ei​ϕ1|010⟩+cosθ1ei​ϕ2|100⟩,\displaystyle|\psi_{1}\rangle=\sin\theta_{1}\sin\theta_{2}|001\rangle+\sin\theta_{1}\cos\theta_{2}e^{i\phi_{1}}|010\rangle+\cos\theta_{1}e^{i\phi_{2}}|100\rangle, (S145)
|ψ2⟩=sinθ3sinθ4|110⟩+sinθ3cosθ4ei​ϕ3|101⟩+cosθ3ei​ϕ4|011⟩.\displaystyle|\psi_{2}\rangle=\sin\theta_{3}\sin\theta_{4}|110\rangle+\sin\theta_{3}\cos\theta_{4}e^{i\phi_{3}}|101\rangle+\cos\theta_{3}e^{i\phi_{4}}|011\rangle.

We first consider the estimation of {θ0,θ1,θ2,ϕ1,ϕ2}\{\theta_{0},\theta_{1},\theta_{2},\phi_{1},\phi_{2}\} in |ψ⟩=sin⁡θ0​|ψ1⟩+cos⁡θ0​ei​ϕ0​|ψ2⟩|\psi\rangle=\sin\theta_{0}|\psi_{1}\rangle+\cos\theta_{0}e^{i\phi_{0}}|\psi_{2}\rangle. In this case FQ=(FQ​1𝟎𝟎FQ​2)F_{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}F_{Q1}&\mathbf{0}\\ \mathbf{0}&F_{Q2}\end{pmatrix} with

FQ​1\displaystyle F_{Q1} =diag⁡{4,4​sin2⁡θ0,4​sin2⁡θ0​sin2⁡θ1},\displaystyle=\operatorname{diag}\{4,4\sin^{2}\theta_{0},4\sin^{2}\theta_{0}\sin^{2}\theta_{1}\}, (S146)
